overview: This four-page confidential consular report from Vice Consul Charles E. Reed II in Taihoku examines the Taiwan Railway Department’s efforts to reverse declining revenue in 1931. It describes proposals to establish feeder bus routes, purchase and eliminate competing private bus companies, and expand successful motor-operated light railway-car services around Taichu and Tainan. The report emphasizes the financial obstacle posed by reduced appropriations but predicts that either policy would create sales opportunities for American manufacturers of buses, engines, and mechanical equipment; its information came from local newspapers and officials of the Railway Department of the Government-General of Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Report on increasing Taiwan Railway Department revenue
subfiles.from: Vice Consul Charles E. Reed II, Taihoku
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State; copy to the Consulate General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report assesses plans to increase railway revenue through feeder buses, the acquisition of competing bus companies, and expanded motor-operated light railway-car services.
subfiles.summary: Facing appreciably declining revenue, the Taiwan Railway Department was considering feeder bus services and the purchase of private bus companies operating routes parallel to the railway, although budget reductions made the necessary capital difficult to obtain. The success of motor-operated light railway cars had already prompted expansion around Taichu and Tainan, and officials were weighing their wider use against parallel bus services. Reed expected both approaches to benefit American exporters because many existing buses required replacement and the light railway cars used American motive units and other mechanical equipment. The report was based on recent local newspaper reports and conversations with responsible Railway Department officials.

interest: The report offers a compact view of how Taiwan’s colonial railway administration responded to competition from road transport during the early 1930s. It is particularly useful for showing that buses were regarded simultaneously as railway competitors and as potential feeder services, while small motorized railcars offered another means of adapting established infrastructure. Its commercial emphasis also reveals how American consular officials translated local transportation policy into prospective export opportunities for U.S. vehicle and machinery manufacturers.
